key_insight: An octopus-inspired soft arm equipped with distributed optoelectronic mechanosensors in its suction cups performs local contact sensing and peripheral control to infer object position and execute autonomous underwater grasps with low latency.
problem_solved: Enables robust underwater manipulation with soft robots by providing dense, local contact sensing and on‑arm inference to overcome limited vision, occlusion, and centralized control delays.
method: Embed optoelectronic mechanosensors into suction cups to measure local contact forces and deformations.
Use sensor arrays distributed along the arm to infer object position and contact state via local signal processing (peripheral inference) rather than relying solely on central vision.
Implement peripheral control policies that combine local sensor feedback and simple reflexes to enable autonomous grasping underwater.
impact: Shows how rich, distributed tactile sensing and edge (peripheral) inference can reduce reliance on heavyweight central perception/control pipelines, enabling faster, more robust manipulation—useful for designing sensor-driven control and learning systems in robotics and edge AI.

paper_title: Peripheral control enabled by distributed sensing in an octopus-inspired soft robotic arm for autonomous underwater grasping
paper_authors: Emanuela Del Dottore, Romina Adhami, Ebrahim Shahabi, Emanuele Solfiti, Michele Martini
